fields.title: Pyltsa: Experiment Came Back Flat
fields.summary: The primary metric didn't move, while two secondary metrics increased. Decide what to do with the module.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do with the module and what will you tell the team?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for recommendations at a marketplace.
fields.brief/company: Pyltsa is a marketplace for used furniture: 2.1 million monthly active users.
fields.brief/context: Six weeks ago, the team launched a new recommendation module on the home screen in a 50/50 test. The primary metric is purchases per visitor. The test ran for four weeks, and the result was flat: +0.4% with a confidence interval from −1.1% to +1.9%. The designer and tech lead want to ship: it looks better, works faster, and two secondary metrics grew. The analyst says the test 'detected no effect'.
fields.brief/objective: Make a decision on the module and justify it.
fields.brief/constraints: Keeping the test running costs nothing directly, but the module blocks two other home screen updates. The analyst is available for one more week.
fields.brief/task: Decide what to do and justify your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A flat result is a result, not a reason to switch metrics
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When the primary metric doesn't move, it's tempting to showcase any secondary metric that did. After that, the team stops trusting experiments — and rightly so. An honest post-mortem looks different: call a flat result flat, identify explainable defects, ship or revert based on a rationale you can say out loud, and document the takeaway along with its bounds.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
The new module replaces the static 'Recently Added' row with a personalized 12-item carousel powered by the existing recommendation engine. It also loads asynchronously — hence the −180 ms.

An unexpected change: the carousel takes up space above the 'Message Seller' button, which used to be above the fold and is now pushed below the fold on most phones.

Moving the button back above the carousel takes two days of work without changing the carousel behavior.

Messaging the seller is the second-to-last step before buying: 71% of purchases start with a message.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Queued behind this module are two other home screen updates: category navigation overhaul (four weeks of dev, finished, waiting for a clean screen to test) and seller ad placements — with a target metric promised for this quarter.

Designer's stance: 'The old row was static and ugly. Even if conversion is flat, the new one is better and faster.'

Tech lead's stance: '180 ms is a real improvement, we fought for it for six months.'

The team keeps no record of past experiments: they were only discussed in meetings.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Fix the button, ship, and test new users separately
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Spend two days moving 'Message Seller' back above the carousel, ship based on engagement and speed improvements, and test the new visitor hypothesis in a separate experiment with a pre-defined metric.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
First, you call out what happened: the primary metric didn't move, and framing secondary metrics as a win means moving goalposts after seeing the numbers.
However, there is an explainable defect: seller messages fell by 5.4%, and 71% of purchases start there. The button slipped below the fold — two days of work.
After fixing it, you ship the module on honest grounds: 180 ms faster, higher engagement, no drop in purchases. The queue of two pending updates is unblocked.
The new-visitor slice is turned into a separate test with a pre-defined metric — as the analyst requested, one significant slice out of six is a question, not an answer.
You create a knowledge card: hypothesis, result, and what it doesn't prove. No records were kept before.
Trade-off: the team wanted to hear 'we won', but heard 'we didn't lose and we know why'.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Extend the test until statistical significance
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The interval still includes 2%. Keep running the test for another four weeks to narrow it down.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Four more weeks produce a narrower interval: +0.3% (−0.6% to +1.2%). This confirms the 2% effect targeted before launch is definitely absent.
It is an honest answer, but an expensive one: navigation overhaul and the ad placement with quarterly targets were held up in queue for those same four weeks.
Meanwhile, the drop in seller messaging harms half the audience for a full eight weeks.
By the end of the second month, you make the exact same decision you could have made immediately.
Trade-off: precision came at the cost of quarterly commitments and extended user friction; however, finishing a test in itself is not an error.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The primary metric didn't move, and one secondary metric degraded. Roll back and unblock the queue.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Rolling back takes a day, unblocking the queue — that part of the decision is correct.
However, rolling back forfeits the 180 ms speed improvement and engagement gains backed by statistically significant confidence intervals.
Most importantly, the true explanation is lost: the drop in seller messages was caused by pushing the button below the fold — a two-day fix, not a flaw inherent to carousels.
A quarter later, someone proposes personalized recommendations again, and there will be no documented evidence to ground the discussion.
Trade-off: a flat result was treated as negative, and an easily fixable issue as a dealbreaker for the entire module.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Ship and declare victory based on secondary metrics
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Views are up 6.2%, saves up 3.1%, both statistically significant. Ship it and present this as a success.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The module ships, the report highlights two significant metrics, and it looks like a success at the review meeting.
A quarter later, the core product metric hasn't moved, and management asks why a 6% engagement lift didn't drive purchases.
There is no answer: success criteria were swapped after seeing the data, making it impossible to tell what was actually validated.
The drop in seller messages goes unnoticed because it was omitted from the report — even though 71% of purchases originate there.
The team treats the next two tests the same way, and within six months nobody trusts experiment results anymore.
Trade-off: a feel-good story was achieved at the expense of experimental integrity.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Comparing hypotheses by appeal rather than reach, impact, and verification cost
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Setting experiment rules after looking at the numbers
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Failing to turn results into documented knowledge with clear boundaries
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Roadmap looks like a timeline of features instead of problems and metrics
